```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 72,
  fig.retina = 1
)
```

This vignette shows what age, period and cohort effects look like on a
hexamap and on a traditional Lexis diagram, alone, in pairs, and all three
together. The rates are simulated with `simulate_apc()` from a log-linear
model,

$$\log \mu_{ap} = \log(\text{baseline}) + f(a) + g(p) + h(c), \qquad c = p - a,$$

where $f$, $g$ and $h$ are the age, period and cohort effects on the log
scale (log rate ratios).

```{r setup}
library(hexamap)
```

## The effects

Each effect has a shape that is easy to tell apart from the others:

- **Age**: rates peak at age 45.
- **Period**: rates rise steeply after 2010, as in an epidemic.
- **Cohort**: people born between 1955 and 1965 have twice the risk of
  other cohorts.

```{r effects}
ages <- 15:70
periods <- 1999:2018

age <- function(a) -((a - 45) / 15)^2
period <- function(p) 0.12 * pmax(p - 2010, 0)
cohort <- function(c) ifelse(c >= 1955 & c <= 1965, log(2), 0)
```

Each pattern below is shown as a Lexis diagram (left) and a hexamap (right),
with the 1960 birth cohort highlighted. Each figure uses its own color scale.

```{r helper}
compare <- function(rates, title) {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), oma = c(0, 0, 1.5, 0))
  on.exit(par(op))
  lexis_map(rates, legend = FALSE, highlight = list(cohort = 1960, col = "white"))
  hexamap(rates, highlight = list(cohort = 1960, col = "white"))
  mtext(title, outer = TRUE, font = 2, cex = 1.2)
}
```

## How to read the isolines

- **Age effects** follow the age isolines: on a hexamap they slope down to
  the right (−30°); on a Lexis diagram they are horizontal.
- **Period effects** follow the period isolines, which are vertical on both.
- **Cohort effects** follow the cohort isolines: on a hexamap they slope up
  to the right (+30°); on a Lexis diagram they are diagonal (45°).

On a hexamap the three directions are equally spaced, so a cohort band is as
easy to follow as an age or period band.

## One effect

```{r age, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap of an age effect: a band of high rates around age 45 runs along the age isolines."}
compare(simulate_apc(ages, periods, age_effect = age), "Age effect")
```

```{r period, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap of a period effect: rates increase from left to right after 2010, in vertical bands."}
compare(simulate_apc(ages, periods, period_effect = period), "Period effect")
```

```{r cohort, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap of a cohort effect: a band of high rates for the 1955 to 1965 birth cohorts runs along the cohort isolines."}
compare(simulate_apc(ages, periods, cohort_effect = cohort), "Cohort effect")
```

The cohort band is the same width as the others on the hexamap, while on
the Lexis diagram it is narrower across and drawn as a staircase of squares.

## Two effects

```{r age-period, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap of age and period effects combined: the age band around 45 brightens after 2010."}
compare(simulate_apc(ages, periods, age_effect = age, period_effect = period),
        "Age and period effects")
```

```{r age-cohort, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap of age and cohort effects combined: the high-risk cohort band is brightest where it crosses age 45."}
compare(simulate_apc(ages, periods, age_effect = age, cohort_effect = cohort),
        "Age and cohort effects")
```

```{r period-cohort, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap of period and cohort effects combined: the high-risk cohort band brightens after 2010."}
compare(simulate_apc(ages, periods, period_effect = period, cohort_effect = cohort),
        "Period and cohort effects")
```

## All three effects

```{r all, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap of age, period and cohort effects combined: the brightest cells are where the high-risk cohorts are around age 45 after 2010."}
apc <- simulate_apc(ages, periods, age_effect = age, period_effect = period,
                    cohort_effect = cohort)
compare(apc, "Age, period and cohort effects")
```

Real data are noisy. With Poisson counts for 50,000 people per cell, the
three effects are still visible:

```{r noise, fig.alt = "Lexis diagram and hexamap of the same three effects with Poisson noise."}
set.seed(2020)
noisy <- simulate_apc(ages, periods, age_effect = age, period_effect = period,
                      cohort_effect = cohort, population = 5e4)
compare(noisy, "Age, period and cohort effects, with noise")
```

## What a hexamap cannot show

Because cohort = period − age, linear trends in age, period and cohort
cannot be separated: this is the APC identification problem. For example, a
linear increase with age and period gives exactly the same rates as a
steeper linear increase with age plus a linear increase with cohort:

```{r identification}
ap <- simulate_apc(ages, periods,
                   age_effect = function(a) 0.02 * a,
                   period_effect = function(p) 0.02 * p)
ac <- simulate_apc(ages, periods,
                   age_effect = function(a) 0.04 * a,
                   cohort_effect = function(c) 0.02 * c)
all.equal(ap, ac)
```

No display can tell these apart. A hexamap shows departures from linearity,
such as the peak, the surge and the high-risk cohorts above, without
distorting any of the three directions. Estimating the separate effects needs
an APC model with an identifying assumption.
